svg.aria-label: Diagram: A CloudWatch Logs data protection policy audits and masks sensitive data in log events. Masking is applied at all egress points, including CloudWatch Logs Insights, metric filters and subscription filters, and only users who have the logs:Unmask IAM permission can view unmasked data, using the unmask parameter on GetLogEvents or FilterLogEvents. That makes the control a read-time transformation rather than redaction: the unmasked value is still retained and one IAM permission returns it, so logs:Unmask is the real control boundary. Masking applies only from the moment the policy exists, because sensitive data is detected and masked when it is ingested into the log group, and log events ingested before that time are not masked, with an account-level policy taking up to five minutes to begin masking in existing log groups. The policy itself is two JSON blocks whose data identifier arrays must exactly match: an Audit action, which is required to find the sensitive data terms and must contain a FindingsDestination object, and a Deidentify action, which is what actually masks the data and must contain an empty MaskConfig object. The findings destination list is optional, so a policy can mask correctly while keeping no durable record of what it found. Audit findings are written one report per log event containing sensitive data, and they contain the log group ARN, the identifier name, a count of occurrences in that event, and the start and end character offsets of each occurrence, but never the sensitive value itself. Destinations must already exist, and an S3 bucket protected with SSE-KMS requires a key policy update so the log delivery account can write to it, while SSE-S3 requires nothing. Detection uses pattern matching and machine learning models, and for some managed data identifiers detection depends on also finding certain keywords in proximity with the sensitive data, so coverage depends on how log messages are phrased; custom data identifiers exist for formats you control. The LogEventsWithFindings metric is emitted in the AWS slash Logs namespace, is free of charge, and counts the number of log events containing sensitive data rather than the number of occurrences, so it is a lower bound on exposure. Account-level and log-group-level policies are cumulative with no exclusion mechanism, each log group may have only one log-group-level policy, the document limit is 30,720 characters, and masking is supported in both the Standard and Essentials log classes.
svg.title: Masking is applied at egress, and logs:Unmask is the real boundary
svg.text: A presentation control over retained data. Not redaction.
“… is masked at all egress points, including CloudWatch Logs Insights, metric filters, and subscription
filters.” And: “Only users who have the logs:Unmask IAM permission can view unmasked data.”
WHAT IT COVERS — EVERY EXIT
Logs Insights queries
metric filters
subscription filters → even the SIEM copy
Genuinely broad: these are the three ways out.
WHAT IT DOES NOT DO
Remove the value from the log group.
logs:Unmask + unmask=true returns it.
So that permission list is the set of identities for
whom your policy does not exist.
It starts when you create it
“When you set a data protection policy, log events ingested to the log group before that time are not masked.”
A policy created after a leak does nothing about the leak. Delete, shorten retention, or rotate instead.
Two blocks, matching identifier lists — and one optional field that decides your evidence
Audit finds the terms · must contain FindingsDestination
Deidentify “what actually masks the data” · MaskConfig must be empty
But the destination LIST is optional — so a policy can mask correctly and record nothing at all.
The arrays must match exactly, which removes the whole class of audit-one-thing-mask-another mistakes.
A FINDING NEVER CARRIES THE VALUE
resourceArn · name · count · start/end offsets
“an email occupied characters 13 to 26” — never which
address. Enough to fix the log line, not to re-leak it.
DETECTION IS NOT A REGEX
“detection depends on also finding certain keywords
in proximity with the sensitive data.”
Coverage depends on how your app phrases its logs.
LogEventsWithFindings is free, and counts EVENTS not occurrences — one event with a thousand records
increments it by one. Treat it as a trigger for “whether”, and read the findings for “how much”.
The policy decides what is hidden. logs:Unmask decides who it is hidden from.
Govern the second as carefully as you configure the first. And it works in the Essentials class, unlike most of Logs.
